prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, and so generate credit cycles in the macroeconomy

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore's 1997 'Credit Cycles' identifies a specific, portable mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to the value of collateral create a feedback loop between asset prices and credit. Small shocks then become large and persistent, and the effects spread across sectors and over time. This changed how macroeconomists model investment, housing and leverage. It is now a standard building block in quantitative macro-finance models, in analyses of the 2008 crisis and in macroprudential policy discussions. The credit is cleanly attributable to two people. The idea is nearly three decades old and has been absorbed into teaching, academic work and central-bank modelling, so there is no timing concern. In my opening ranking it was the clearest conceptual advance with the cleanest attribution among the shortlisted candidates, and the colleagues' arguments have not changed that.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness and validation. The 2022 prize recognised banks and financial crises, and a committee could see this as the same territory. The amplification mechanism is also validated more through later quantitative and empirical work by others than through direct identification in the original contribution. A further risk is that the prize would reward a theoretical mechanism while candidates such as B005 have a more documented record in everyday policy practice. Taken together, these may make B027 look less compelling to colleagues who weight demonstrated policy use or direct causal evidence more heavily.

responses.point: Per Strömberg ranked B027 seventh and proposed adding Mark Gertler as a third laureate for the financial accelerator, while noting that this line is shared with Bernanke, who was recognised in 2022, and that Gertler also appears on B036.
responses.response: I see the logic of covering the accelerator line, and Gertler's work matters. I still prefer two names. The Bernanke-Gertler mechanism works through agency costs and borrower net worth. Kiyotaki-Moore's mechanism is dynamic and works through collateral values and asset-price feedback. Putting them in one citation blurs the discovery being rewarded. It also brings in the Bernanke overlap that Strömberg himself flags, and Gertler's credit is already spread across B036. If the Committee wants the empirical side of the accelerator literature, I would treat that as a different case rather than a third name here. I accept that this choice gives up some breadth.

responses.point: Kerstin Enflo ranked B027 eighth, citing its closeness to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises and noting that empirical validation of the amplification mechanism is indirect.
responses.response: I agree that the empirical validation is indirect, and that is the weakest part of my case. I do not think the 2022 overlap is as close as she suggests. The 2022 prize concerned bank runs, the role of banks in intermediation and the Great Depression evidence. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how borrowers' collateral constraints turn shocks into macroeconomic fluctuations. The topics are adjacent, but the contributions differ. A fair reading is that the overlap is a risk the Committee should weigh. I do not read it as disqualifying. The later empirical work on collateral and investment, and on housing and credit cycles, mostly supports the mechanism's relevance. I remain uncertain how much weight indirect validation should carry for a theory contribution of this age.

responses.point: Richard Friberg ranked B005 first. His main argument is that demand-estimation and dynamic-industry methods now underpin merger review, antitrust, trade, health and environmental analysis, so their reach goes well beyond IO.
responses.response: This is the strongest competing argument, and it moved me. I had ranked B005 last, mainly because I thought attribution was diffuse. Several colleagues, Friberg among them, converge on a Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes core. That reduces my attribution concern, though Friberg's own choice of Bresnahan over Levinsohn shows the boundary is still contested. I would apply his breadth-of-use criterion equally to Kiyotaki-Moore, whose mechanism is also embedded in policy-oriented and quantitative models. I would not rank a toolkit above a conceptual mechanism simply because the toolkit has more documented applications. I am not an IO specialist, so I defer to colleagues with that expertise on the Levinsohn-Bresnahan question. That is why B005 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Randi Hjalmarsson ranked B030 first. She argued that Katz belongs to the skill-bias and education-race strand that is closely tied to the already-recognised Goldin work, and that the China-shock design is a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson contribution.
responses.response: This qualifies my opening proposal of Autor, Hanson and Katz. I had treated Dorn as the most plausible omission. Her point that the China-shock design is a joint contribution and that Katz's strand overlaps the 2023 prize persuades me that Dorn should be preferred over Katz if B030 is pursued. I still keep B030 only as an alternative. The debate over the size and persistence of the trade-shock effects continues, and the task framework owes a good deal to people outside the credited set.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats Kiyotaki-Moore as distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, or as too close to it.
How much weight indirect empirical validation of the amplification mechanism should carry compared with candidates that have a documented policy and measurement record, such as B005.
Whether the Committee would want a third name (Gertler or Gilchrist) to cover the financial-accelerator line, or whether two names give the cleaner citation.

The relative merit of a conceptual-mechanism prize (B027) against a methods and toolkit prize (B005). My own ranking of B005 was affected by my doubts about attribution, and I have not verified these judgements against outside sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from my profile. My profile shows that I am a long-running co-author of Peter Klenow (credited on B046, which is not in my preferred configuration) and a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and of John Hassler (chair). I am also an IIES colleague of both. Krusell and Hassler both ranked B027 highly, so my agreement with them should not be read as independent confirmation. Nothing in the supplied profile requires recusal from the preferred part.
